If they were sitting on this, they would try to minimize the damage and would try to warn the public to start moving to more secure encryption schemes because they know there’s a ticking time bomb until its public anyway. That’s not to say that it won’t happen in the next few weeks. I just don’t think it’s happened yet.

comments.text:
Bruno Latour wrote in Science in Action about "centers of calculation" being critical to scientific advancement. His example was the monumental world changing work Tycho Brahe did pulling together every astronomical calculation, star map, prediction then normalizing, regularizing, and combining them on his island of Oueneberg.
Without this work getting data organized, Kepler couldn't have worked out the planetary laws of motion and then the Copernican Revolution came thereafter.
What we're witnessing is a similar moment. What transformers were able to achieve was a systematic way of normalizing and combining all human data. There will be a lot of progress in the short term. And then more problems will reveal themselves. There will be A LOT of work coming out of this.

This is the single most important attack vector for SAAS companies. It has been for a long time --- this is the standard fact pattern for every SAAS breach --- but much more so today. As the number of employees grow, the likelihood that one of their laptops will get compromised approaches 1. When that happens, the attacker will be able to push code to Github, and if that code gets deployed, you're owned.
In 1Password's case, the absolute worst-case catastrophe is mitigated by the fact that customers retain custody of their unlocking secrets; 1Password (at least in the normal product flows) simply doesn't hold it. But an attack like this implicates every catastrophe short of that worst case.
Change velocity in 2026 is unreal and that trend is going to continue. You could not outcompete 1Password by building a handcrafted artisanal password manager backend (witness all the commercially successful password managers that don't even share 1Password's customer secret custody model). I work in the creative tools space.
This is one of the biggest issues right now. It's nearly impossible to separate "this image was fully generated with AI" versus "I made a minor edit to the colors or did a cutout or improved the layout with AI" when the endpoint is an image.
Especially for socials, if your brand is an authoritative source, getting hit with a dreaded "AI generated content" tag on instagram or facebook is a death blow to your credibility.
Design tools are in a very hard space because of it. You want to make edits as seamless as possible for users, but your final result can't include any pixels from a generative model. It's a strange dance.

> I solve 79 × 123 by entering the first operand and then turning the crank three times to load 79 × 3 into the accumulator. Next, I shift the accumulator carriage one decimal digit to the right and crank twice; because the accumulator is offset from the input register, this has the same effect as cranking twenty times in the original position; in other words, I add 79 × 20. comments.author: orbital-decay

Terminal giving you a janky and limited remotely accessible canvas you can abuse to make primitive GUIs doesn't imply that "SSH is a GUI framework".
A lot better solution would be designing a compact, semantic, styling-independent remote access protocol that doesn't need bitmaps (unlike most currently available protocols), and uses good compression for actual pictures/videos. That would make any GUI efficiently usable remotely through an adapter for an existing GUI framework, without extra bloat the browser has.

comments.author: xxpor
comments.text:
For TUIs, I wish a 5250-style block based terminal had won over VT100 stream based terminals.
For those not familiar, with a block oriented terminal, the native "chunk" of data is an entire screen. So you can put information in there like "this is a text box". This allows, for example, you to move around the screen with tab and type _with no round trip back to the server_. There's 0 latency. Data is only sent when you hit enter.
On high latency or flaky connections the experience is a million times better.
